claims.text: High configurational entropy in noble-metal HEA nanocatalysts induces marked lattice distortion.
High configurational entropy produces a uniform, chemically homogeneous near-surface environment in noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Lattice distortion and near-surface homogeneity stabilize defect sites and promote charge redistribution.
The proposed entropy-associated structural and electronic features suppress nanoparticle sintering and catalytic deactivation under reaction conditions.
Noble-metal HEA nanocatalysts consequently have superior and more reliable catalytic performance than conventional bimetallic catalysts.
Near-equimolar Au-Pt-Pd-Ru-Ag nanoparticles can be synthesized as a single phase with minimal compositional segregation.
A five-component Au-Pt-Pd-Ru-Ag HEA and a two-component Au-Pt catalyst can be prepared with similar overall elemental composition and nanoparticle size.
Oxidation or hydrogenation at 300–600 K under oxidizing or reducing atmospheres represents typical moderate-temperature catalytic conditions for the proposed materials.
The high-entropy state gives rise to lattice distortion, near-surface chemical homogeneity, and defect-site stabilization.
High configurational entropy creates a rugged energy landscape that causes significant lattice distortion.
The entropy-induced lattice distortion yields uniformly distributed active sites with favorable charge redistribution.
Enhanced defect-recombination dynamics inhibit sintering and restructuring of noble-metal HEA nanoparticles during catalysis.
Under reaction conditions, the noble-metal HEA nanoparticles will retain their single-phase structure and active defect sites better than the bimetallic baseline.
The noble-metal HEA nanoparticles will exhibit higher turnover frequency than the bimetallic nanoparticles.
The noble-metal HEA nanoparticles will exhibit lower activation energy than the bimetallic nanoparticles.
The noble-metal HEA nanoparticles will exhibit longer catalytic stability and less sintering than the bimetallic nanoparticles.
Conventional bimetallic nanoparticles have lower configurational entropy and less pronounced lattice distortion than the proposed five-component HEA nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism should hold for 3–10 nm particles at 300–600 K in both oxidizing and reducing catalytic environments.
The quantitative contributions of lattice distortion and surface homogeneity to activity and stability are not established independently of other surface-electronic effects.
Failure to observe significantly higher activity, reduced particle growth, and longer operational stability in the HEA would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The proposed HEA is a five-component Au-Pt-Pd-Ru-Ag material, whereas the baseline is two-component Au-Pt, so the two sets cannot simultaneously have matching or similar overall elemental compositions as stated. This also prevents composition from being held constant while varying only configurational entropy.
